result:
I'll write about something that's been on my mind lately: the strange intimacy of public spaces, and how we carry our private lives through corridors of collective experience.

---

There's a particular quality to the light in hospital waiting rooms at six in the morning. It filters through windows that haven't been cleaned in months, carrying the gray-blue of a winter dawn that hasn't committed to becoming day. I've spent too many hours in these rooms, and I've come to believe they're among the most honest spaces in our built environment. Nowhere else do we sit so openly with our fear, our boredom, our hope, our bodies in various states of malfunction. The magazines are always outdated. The coffee is always terrible. And yet people talk to each other in waiting rooms with a directness that would seem invasive anywhere else. A woman once told me about her daughter's miscarriage while we waited for CT results. She'd never mention it at a dinner party. The fluorescent lighting and institutional chairs stripped away the usual choreography.

I've been thinking about these liminal zones—airports, laundromats, highway rest stops, the lines at the DMV—where we're thrown together without the usual social scripts. The anthropologist Marc Augé called them "non-places," but I think he got it backwards. They're intensely *placed*, intensely present. It's our homes that have become the non-places, the spaces of dissociation, scrolling through feeds while half-watching television, the body parked somewhere comfortable while attention fragments across time zones.

The laundromat at midnight is a cathedral of this inverted intimacy. I used to go to one on Belmont Avenue in Chicago, a narrow storefront with machines that shook like they were trying to escape their own metal shells. The attendant, a man named Ernesto who'd been there fifteen years, kept a space heater behind the counter and read detective novels in Spanish. He knew everyone's business without ever asking. He knew who was washing bedsheets because they'd finally left a partner, who was cleaning sleeping bags because they lived in their car, who was washing everything they owned because of bed bugs, who was just a college student procrastinating on a paper. The machines turned, and we all sat with our damp lives tumbling in the dryers.

I want to write about the woman I saw once at a rest stop in Ohio, somewhere between Columbus and Cincinnati. It was three in the morning, and I was driving back from a funeral, that particular exhaustion where grief and caffeine create a strange alertness. She was standing at the vending machines in a nightgown, a long blue flannel thing, with a winter coat thrown over it and boots with the laces untied. She was trying to get a bag of chips to drop, hitting the machine with the heel of her hand, not angry but rhythmic, like she was negotiating with a stubborn animal. I bought a coffee and watched from the corner. Eventually she got her chips. She sat in one of the molded plastic chairs and ate them slowly, looking at nothing, her hair still flattened on one side from sleep. I never knew her story. She never knew I was watching, or if she did, she didn't care. That moment of her life, that private act of needing something salty at three in the morning in a public corridor, existed complete without my understanding it. I carry it anyway.

We're told that modern life is alienating, that we've lost the village square, the front porch, the communal bath. But I think we've developed different forms of being together, stranger and perhaps more fragile. The person who recognizes you at the coffee shop and starts your order when you walk in. The neighbor whose name you don't know but whose schedule you could set your watch by, who leaves at 7:12 every morning with a dog that pulls toward the hydrant. The collective held breath in a subway car when someone faints, the sudden emergency democracy of strangers deciding who knows CPR, who will call, who will hold the person's hand.

There's a violence to this too, of course. The same subway car holds harassment, the unhoused person everyone pretends not to see, the racial profiling that determines who gets asked for their ticket. Public space is where our social failures become visible, where inequality moves from abstraction to the body sitting next to you, smelling of unwashed clothes, talking to voices you can't hear. The honesty of these spaces cuts both ways. We can't look away, or we learn to look away with a skill that becomes its own wound.

I keep returning to the idea that we're always performing versions of ourselves, but the performances get thinner in certain lights. The hospital waiting room, the all-night laundromat, the rest stop at the edge of exhaustion—these are stages where the repertory company of our social selves goes on strike, and something more ragged appears. Not the "authentic self" of self-help mythology, which is just another performance with better marketing. Something more interesting: the self in abeyance, the self in waiting, the self that doesn't know what comes next.

Ernesto at the laundromat died last year, I heard. Someone else runs it now, keeps the fluorescent lights on all night, but doesn't read behind the counter. I think about him when I pass the place, now converted to a more expensive operation with an app to check machine availability. The inefficiency was the point, I want to tell the developers. The waiting was the point. The space to be nowhere in particular, with others similarly unmoored, was the point.

I started this thinking I'd write about something else entirely. That's another intimacy of writing, I suppose: the way your fingers on keys make decisions your planning mind hasn't approved. The essay becomes its own non-place, a corridor where thoughts tumble together without the usual domestic arrangements. You're here with me in it, whoever you are, reading at some hour I can't imagine, carrying your own rest stops and laundromats and waiting rooms. We've never met. For this moment, that doesn't matter. The light is gray-blue, not quite committed to becoming day. The machines turn. We wait, together, for what comes next.
